On a like-for-like 2026Q2 basis the spread is 6.3% to 8.78%, or 2.48 points across six brokers [F102][F81].

**Why they differ:**

- **Numerator definition.** A vacancy rate is availability — or vacant space only, depending on the broker — as a share of stock. Brokers that count marketed space with a forward completion horizon will read higher than those counting only space physically vacant today. The store holds no per-broker definition for this metric (the definition field is empty on every row), so the exact split can't be pinned to a named broker, but this is the standard cause of a gap of this size.
- **Denominator.** Brokers' stock totals and boundaries differ, which alone can move the rate by a point or more.
- **Timing.** Part of the apparent disagreement is simply vintage: JLL's newest reading is 2026Q3 at 8.3% [F51] versus 8.6% in Q2 [F60], and CBRE [F125] and Savills [F45] have moved to August monthlies (6.7% and 7.0%, from 6.5% [F117] and 7.2% [F32] in Q2). Vacancy is drifting down, so older quarterly figures sit above newer ones.
- **Not boundaries.** Every row's area fit is exact — all six are measuring the same Central London geography, so the spread is not a submarket-mapping artefact.

**House view:** Central London vacancy sits in a 6.3%–8.78% range across brokers. For conservative underwriting of voids and re-letting risk, work from the top of the range (Cushman & Wakefield 8.78% [F81], JLL 8.3% [F51], BNP Paribas 8.4% [F5]); the lower readings from Avison Young [F102] and CBRE [F125] better reflect space physically empty today, and the direction of travel — down in every broker's latest print — matters more than the level.

The reasons the committee gave [D194#3]:

Our screening checklist treats a loan taken out around 2017–18 for five years as a priority profile [D197#2].

The card-decision log returned no comparable earlier decisions for this asset. If Example House returns through administration, the price and EPC objections are the ones to re-test.
